parole.significato: Added mostly to adjectives ending in -as and -us to form nouns indicating a state of being, similar to (and frequently…
parole.testo: From Proto-Baltic *-umas, possibly from an earlier suffix *-ma(s) added to a u-stem (e.g., Lithuanian saugùs (“safe, sure”), saugù-mas), from which the u was reinterpreted as part of the suffix and then extended to other stems. Compare Samogitian -oms, Latvian -ums.

Per Girdenis, probably from an unattested Proto-Baltic *au̯ikā́ (“sheep”), with syncope of the *-i-, from a diminutive of Proto-Balto-Slavic *áwis (“sheep”), and exact cognate with Proto-Slavic *ovьcà (“sheep”), Sanskrit अविका (avikā́, “ewe”). The word experienced semantic shift from "sheep" > "sacr
From Proto-Baltic *balsas, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-s- (“to sound”). Cognate with Latvian balss and Latgalian bolss.

Postverbal back-formation from *brandyti (“to mature, ripen”), from Proto-Baltic *brand-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrond-, possibly a nasal extension of *bʰer- (“to bear”). Compare Latvian briedums (“mature”).

From Proto-Baltic *deš-, and cognate with Latvian dȩsa (“sausage”). The further origin of the root is unclear; Smoczynski refrains from assigning any etymology, while Karulis derives the root from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to cut, to sever, to split into fibers”). In the latter case, compare diale

From Pre-Lithuanian *dēvas, from Proto-Baltic *deiṷas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *deiwás (compare Latvian dievs, Old Prussian Deiwas), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós. Cognate to English Tiw, Latin deus, Irish dia, Breton doue, Welsh duw, Persian دیو, Parthian 𐫅𐫏𐫇 (dyw) Avestan 𐬛𐬀𐬉𐬎𐬎𐬀 (daēuua), Sogdi

From Proto-Baltic *drans- (with a nasal infix), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰers- (“to be courageous”). Cognate with Latvian drošs, Old Prussian dirsos, Polish dziarski, Ancient Greek θρασύς (thrasús).

Inherited from Proto-Baltic *dumblás, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”) via nasal infixation. Cognate with Latvian dumbla (dialectal), dubļi pl (“mud”), perhaps further akin to Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ (“oak”).

Cognate with Latvian ē̃rce, from Proto-Baltic [Term?], of unknown ultimate origin. Compare Proto-Slavic *ràkъ ~ *òrkъ (“crayfish”), in which case a doublet of rõkis; possibly from an extinct substrate language.
From Proto-Baltic *ežis, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *eźjás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis (“hedgehog”). Cognate with Latvian ezis and Proto-Slavic *ežь.
From Proto-Baltic *gais- or *gaid-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gaid-sus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēy-, *gʷʰəy- (“bright, shining”) with an extra -s.

From Proto-Baltic *gil- (compare Latvian dziļš (“deep”)), of unknown further origin. Various proposed theories, including those relating the word to Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to hurt, stab”) (whence gélti (“to ache, sting, bite”) and Proto-Germanic *kwelaną (“to suffer, hurt”)), are semantically

From Proto-Baltic *gim-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥-, the zero grade form of *gʷem- (“to go, to come, to step”), with semantic shift "to come (into the world)" > "to be born"; note that the word does not seem to descend from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth, produce”) (the usual "born
From Proto-Baltic *grenž- (compare Latvian griezt (“to turn, spin”)), from Proto-Indo-European *grenǵʰ- (“to turn, spin”), whence also Proto-Germanic *kringaną (“to turn, fall, yield”).

From Proto-Baltic, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jaudīˀtei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hyéwdʰh₁eti (“to move forward”), or a root *Hyewdʰ-, derived from *h₂yew-. Compare Sanskrit युध्यते (yúdhyate, “to battle”).
From Proto-Baltic *jḗˀgāˀ, from *yēgʷeh₂ (“power, youthful strength”). Cognates include Latvian jȩ̃ga (“meaning, sense, point”), Ancient Greek ἥβη (hḗbē, “power, youthful strength”).
From Proto-Baltic *jáuˀrāˀ.

parole.significato: war (conflict involving organized use of arms)
parole.testo: From Proto-Baltic *karjas, from Proto-Indo-European *kóryos (“war, troops”), from the root *ker- (“army”). Cognate with Latvian karš (“war”), Old Prussian kargis (“troops, army”).

From Proto-Baltic *kerp-, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to pluck, harvest”), a form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut, chop”). Cognate with Latvian cìrpt (“to shave”), Proto-Slavic *čerpti (“to scoop, draw (water, etc.)”), Latin carpo (“to seize”), and, from *(s)ker-, a multitude of other

parole.significato: to bite hard, to crunch, to chomp
parole.testo: From a series of onomatopoeic words which trace to a Proto-Baltic *krimt-. Cognate with Latvian krimst (“to bite, separate”).

From Proto-Baltic *kur, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷór. Cognate with Samogitian kor, Latvian kur, Latgalian kur, Old Prussian quei, Proto-Slavic *kъde, Sanskrit कुत्र (kútra), Latin cūr (“why”), cubī, Albanian ku.

Cognate with Old Prussian quoitā (“wants”), quoi (“(I/you) want”), quāits (“desire”), from a Proto-Baltic *kwit-, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire, seek”) and cognate with Latin quaerō (“to seek, question”). Older comparisons to Lithuanian káitėti (“to lack, be wanting”), Old Ea

From Proto-Baltic *leyt- (whence also Latvian làitît (“to rub, whip, massage, caress”)), of uncertain further origin. Buck implicitly derives the Baltic from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”) (by comparing to Latin linō (“to daub, anoint”)), while Chantraine, Pokorny, and Smoczynski tentativ

From Proto-Baltic *linksmas, synchronically analyzable as an adjectival formation in -mas from links-, itself a formation from liñkti (“to bend, bow”) (see also linkė́ti (“to wish”)). The sense development would be along the lines of "flexible, bowing" > "expressing one's best wishes" > "acceptable"

From Proto-Baltic *tlāk- (with reduction of the “difficult” cluster tl to l), and cognate with Latvian lācis, Old Prussian clokis (klokis) (< *tlokis), Tlokunpelk (“Prussian placename”, literally “bear swamp”), Sudovian łukas. The term replaced the original word for bear, Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱ
From Proto-Baltic *mak-, from Proto-Indo-European *mak- (“small (leather) bag or pouch”), see also Russian мошна (mošna, “purse, pouch”).

From Proto-Baltic *meit- (“to feed on”), and cognate with Latvian mist (“id”). The Baltic root seems to further derive from a Proto-Indo-European *meyt(h)-, though cognates are debated. Pokorny equated the root to *meyth₂- (“to exchange”), taking the primary meaning as "abode, dwelling-place"; Derks

parole.significato: to be able to; to know how
parole.testo: Cognate with Latvian mâcêt (“to be able to, know”), from Proto-Baltic *maˀk-, with further etymology unclear. Potential affinities to Ancient Greek μῆχος (mêkhos, “means, expedient”) and Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”) are semantically appealing, but unconvincing on formal grounds. The "to
Along with magėti (“to please, interest”), from Proto-Baltic *mog-, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *moťì (“to be able”).

From Proto-Baltic *melˀ(n)- (“black, blue”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-(n-) (“dark, red, dirty”). Cognates include Latvian melns (“black”), Old Prussian melne (“bruise”), Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “dark, black”) (whence English melanin). Probably akin to Proto-Slavic *malina (“raspberry”).

Cognate with Lithuanian nerštas, Latvian nārsts (“spawning”), Latvian nārstot (“to spawn”), from Proto-Baltic [Term?] and Proto-Balto-Slavic *nerṣ-t-. Compare Russian нерест (nerest), Proto-Slavic *nerstъ.

From Proto-Baltic *pā́ˀinas, from Proto-Indo-European *poyHnos, *peyHnos (“milk, fat”). Cognate with Latvian piẽns (“milk”), Sanskrit पयस् (páyas, “milk”), Persian پینو (pînû, “butter-milk”). Related to dialectal Samogitian pýti (“to start to give milk”) (< Proto-Indo-European zero-grade *piH-).
From Proto-Baltic *plauˀtá, from Proto-Indo-European *plew-. Cognate with Latvian plàukts (“shelf, sideboard of a bee-hive”)

parole.significato: to get accustomed, to get used to
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Baltic *prastei, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pret- (“to interpret”). Cognate with Latvian prast.
From Proto-Baltic *pēdā́ˀ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pēd-ó (“to walk; foot”). Cognate with Latvian pēda (“foot-sole”), Old Prussian pedan (“plowshare”).
From Proto-Baltic *p(o)ut- (which appears to be sound-symbolic), with seemingly no cognates outside of Baltic. Cognate with Latvian pùst (“to blow”).

From Proto-Baltic *rūp-, an extended zero-grade form of Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to pull, to tear, to break”). The sense development would be "to tear, break" > "to emotionally break" > "to worry" > "to care, concern"; a semantic parallel is found in Polish troska (“care, worry”), from Proto-Sl

From Proto-Baltic *sek-, *sak-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sákīˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to say”). Cognate to Latvian sacīt, Russian сочить (sočitʹ, “to emit (a liquid)”), German sagen (“to say”), English say and Latin inquam (“to say”). Compare sekti (“to follow”) from e-grade *sekʷ- (“
From siaũbas (“fear, terror”) + -i̇̀ngas, derivative of siaũbti (“to devastate”), from Proto-Baltic *siaup-, from Proto-Indo-European *sewp- (“to throw, pour over”).

From Proto-Baltic *skan-; cognate with Latvian skans (“sour”) and possibly Old Prussian stanulonx (“red-flowered scallion known for its pungent taste”), the latter which is probably a mistranscription or other such corruption of an unattested *scanulonx. Further origin unclear; the word may be deriv

From Proto-Baltic *skerd-ti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerdʰ- (“to cut”), an extension of *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Cognate with Latvian šķērst (“to dissect”), Middle High German scherzen (“to cut off, shorten”), Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), Proto-Slavic *skorda (“harrow”); see also Lithuanian s

From Proto-Baltic *smag-, and cognate with Latvian smags (“heavy”). The further interpretation of the root and its deduced extra-Baltic cognates is unclear. Traditionally held to be related to Ancient Greek μογέω (mogéō, “to toil, suffer”); Windekens also adduces Tocharian B māsk- (“to be difficult”
From Proto-Baltic [Term?], ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snigʷʰ- (“to snow”). Compare Latvian snigt.

From Proto-Baltic *swetyas, from Proto-Indo-European *swe-tio-s, which is probably a derivative of *swe (“self”). Cognate with Latvian svešs (“strange, foreign”), Proto-Slavic *svatъ (“father of newlyweds”), Proto-Slavic *posětiti (“to visit”), Ancient Greek ἔτης (étēs, “private person”)

parole.significato: seed (the reproductive organ of flowering plants)
parole.testo: From Proto-Baltic *sētl-ā-, a collective formation from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁tlom, from *seh₁- + *-tlom. Cognate with Latvian sēkla. See also sė́ti.

From Old Lithuanian ungurỹs, from Proto-Baltic [Term?], from Proto-Balto-Slavic *angurjás (compare Old Prussian angurgis, Polish węgorz), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engʷʰ-ur-yos (compare Lithuanian ankštiras, inkšti̇̀ras (“pimple; tapeworm”), German Engerling (“maggot”), Albanian thnegël (“ant”)),
From Proto-Baltic *āpē-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep- (“(body of) water”). Cognate with Latvian upe (“river”), Old Prussian apē (“river”), Sudovian upa (“river”).

From Proto-Baltic *žírˀnjas, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źírˀnan, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Compare Latvian zirnis, Old Prussian syrne, Russian зерно́ (zernó), Persian خرمن (xarman), English corn, Italian grano.
According to Weiss, from Proto-Baltic *žvak-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰʷokʷ-, *ǵʰweh₂k- (“to shine”), cognate with Latin fax (“torch”).

Cognate with Latvian ods, from Proto-Baltic *uodas. Further etymology uncertain, but it may be linked with either Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to bite”) or an o-grade of *h₁ed- (“to eat”).
